clue.text: It's right to tuck into meat in a flash

indicators.note: to tuck one thing into another is to put it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: steak is a cut of meat
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone says a sauce or garnish slips into the meat dish in no time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a flash' reads as 'quickly', but only 'a flash' is the definition; 'in' just joins it on.
explanation.definitionFit: A streak is a quick flash, as in a streak of lightning, a single bright line across the sky.

clue.text: Stork, half dead, in trouble could be massaged

indicators.note: only half of the following word is kept, the other half being dropped
letters in trouble are in disorder, so they are mixed up into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, before its second half goes

explanation.surface: A stork, near death and in distress, might be soothed with a gentle massage.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of DEAD is DE; STORK plus DE is then rearranged into STROKED.
explanation.definitionFit: To stroke is to rub gently with the hand, which is a light form of massaging.

clue.text: Hark at this! Free 'air-do!

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe and hyphen

explanation.surface: A cockney cry, mocking a free hairdo with a dropped aitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air-do is a dropped-aitch spelling of hairdo, there only to supply five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A radio is something you listen to, so 'Hark at this!' is what you might say pointing to one.

clue.text: Versatile one needs dressing up, having to propose

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

blocks.note: a means one, as in a single thing
a pad is a wound dressing
in British usage, to table a motion is to propose it for discussion

explanation.surface: Someone adaptable is advised to dress smartly before popping the question.
explanation.walkthrough: PAD reversed gives DAP; A + DAP + TABLE. In the UK, tabling a motion puts it forward, whereas in the US it shelves it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something adaptable can adjust to many uses, which is what being versatile means.

clue.text: A sewer may need this labour and land

blocks.note: work is labour
to land a catch is to bag it

explanation.surface: It looks like a drain or sewage pipe requiring labour and land to build.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as a drain, but here it is someone who sews.
explanation.definitionFit: A workbag holds needles, thread and other sewing materials, so a person who sews would want one.

clue.text: Bereaved woman, almost an idol, needing to marry

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off

blocks.note: W is an abbreviation for woman or women
taken as written, before its last letter goes
to wed is to marry

explanation.surface: A grieving woman, nearly worshipped, must find a new husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman' reads as the definition, but it is only a single-letter abbreviation; the definition is 'Bereaved'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone widowed has lost a spouse to death, which is one form of being bereaved.

clue.text: Firearm that removes the top of nothing

indicators.note: removing the top of a down entry takes away its first letter

blocks.note: a trifle is something of no importance, next to nothing

explanation.surface: A gun that blows the head off nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIFLE without its first letter gives RIFLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a long-barrelled gun, a type of firearm.

clue.text: Talked foolishly having foam or froth in bed

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so these letters go within the outer word

blocks.note: taken as written; it is split to hold the other piece
lather is soapy foam or froth

explanation.surface: Someone rambles nonsense while foaming at the mouth in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To blather is to talk at length without much sense, i.e. to talk foolishly.

clue.text: When will they leave? Reckon it's about time!

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer word wraps round the other piece

blocks.note: to reckon is to guess
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A weary host wonders when the visitors will go, deciding it's high time.
explanation.walkthrough: T goes inside GUESS to give GUESTS; the question is the host's weary thought.
explanation.definitionFit: Visitors are the people a host hopes will leave, so the question describes them indirectly.

clue.text: Safe to swallow, perhaps, but I bleed like this

indicators.note: the setter points to the letters rearranged as shown, so they form a new word

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sword swallower notes the act may be safe, yet they still bleed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something edible can be eaten without harm, so it is fit to swallow.

clue.text: In the act of committing a misdeed that's bloody?

definitions.text: In the act of committing a misdeed

blocks.clueFragment: In the act of committing a misdeed
blocks.note: first meaning: caught in the act of wrongdoing
second meaning, literally: having hands red with blood

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom comes from being caught with blood still on your hands, which is the literal second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Caught red-handed is the idiom for being discovered mid-crime, while the literal sense is hands stained red.

clue.text: Arrange false evidence against a skeleton

blocks.note: first meaning: to set someone up for a crime they did not commit
second meaning: a structural framework

explanation.surface: Someone plants evidence to pin a crime on a skeleton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Against a skeleton' looks like one phrase, but the split comes after 'against'.
explanation.definitionFit: To frame someone is to fabricate guilt, and a frame is also the bare supporting structure of something.

clue.text: Whip half a knee out

indicators.note: keeping only half of a word means the rest is cut away

blocks.note: taken as written, before its second half goes
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to whip a kneecap halfway out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of KNEE is KN, followed by OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A knout is a heavy whip once used for flogging in Russia, so it is a kind of whip.

clue.text: Retire a cricketer leading to endless hate

definitions.note: a verb defining a noun: to be given one's bowler hat is British slang for leaving the army

indicators.note: endless means without its end, so the last letter is cut off

blocks.note: a bowler is a cricketer who delivers the ball
taken as written, before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A cricketer's retirement brings on endless bitterness.
explanation.walkthrough: In British military slang, to get your bowler hat means to retire into civilian life, so the definition is loose: a bowler hat is a round hard felt hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Retired British officers traditionally swapped uniform caps for the civilian bowler, so the hat stands for retirement.

clue.text: A small amount of liquid seen on the hockey field?

blocks.note: first meaning: a trickle
second meaning: running with the ball under close control

explanation.surface: A little puddle of spilt drink found on a hockey pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second meaning as an example: players do this in hockey as in football.
explanation.definitionFit: A dribble is a thin trickle of liquid, and also the skill of moving the ball along in short taps.

clue.text: It's silly to hug Mother, but it's natural

indicators.note: something that hugs wraps its arms around another, so the outer word encloses the other

blocks.note: silly means idiotic
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: Someone argues that embracing your mum may look foolish yet is perfectly normal.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'It's' is only a link; 'silly' alone supplies the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic language sounds native and unforced, the way a natural speaker would say it.

clue.text: Shy unfinished act when knocking rum back

indicators.note: unfinished means the final letter is missing
going back means reading the word from right to left
knocking in, as with a nail, drives one thing into another

blocks.note: a deed is an act
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bashful drinker leaves a deed half done while downing rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocking' reads as criticising the drink, but it means knocking in, as with a nail.
explanation.definitionFit: A demure person is modest and reserved, which is close to being shy.

clue.text: Cat seen in the breakfast room?

definitions.text: Cat seen in the breakfast room?

blocks.clueFragment: Cat seen in the breakfast room?
blocks.note: surface reading: a pet wandering in at breakfast time
setter's reading: a ginger cat colour shares its name with an orange spread eaten at breakfast

explanation.walkthrough: A ginger tabby is called a marmalade cat, and the orange preserve is a British breakfast staple on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an orange-coloured cat and the citrus preserve found on the breakfast table.

clue.text: Master has to appreciate unruly set

indicators.note: unruly letters will not stay in line, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: to dig something is slang for appreciating it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster must learn to value an unruly class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master' looks like a teacher, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To digest information is to absorb and understand it fully, i.e. to master it.

clue.text: Voucher to go round hospital hidden in the trees

definitions.note: a group of trees, the plural noun standing for the collective

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so the outer word wraps the other

blocks.note: a ticket is a voucher
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A coupon wrapped around a hospital, tucked away in woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: H goes inside TICKET after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: A thicket is a dense cluster of trees or bushes, so it is the trees where something is hidden.

clue.text: Weariness makes you embarrassed and swell externally

indicators.note: acting externally means on the outside, so that word surrounds the other

blocks.note: to boom is to swell or grow rapidly
embarrassment makes you go red

explanation.surface: Tiredness leaves you flushed and puffy.
explanation.definitionFit: Boredom is the weary, listless feeling of having nothing interesting to do.

clue.text: Graduate and fool must co-exist on fruit

blocks.note: a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
a nana is British slang for a fool

explanation.surface: A student and a clown have to live on fruit alone.
explanation.walkthrough: A nana is informal British for a silly person.
explanation.definitionFit: A banana is a long curved tropical fruit, so it is an example of fruit.

clue.text: Reserve designs; then duty is half done

indicators.note: half done means only part remains, so half the word is dropped

blocks.note: modes are designs or fashions
taken as written, before its first half goes

explanation.surface: Someone sets aside plans, then leaves their work only half finished.
explanation.walkthrough: Here it is the back half of the word that survives, not the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Reserve as a noun means restraint in manner, and modesty is that quality of not putting oneself forward.

clue.text: Picture-maker's equipment (waterproof) turned up on time

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

blocks.note: a mac, short for mackintosh, is a British word for a raincoat
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A photographer's kit, in a waterproof case, arrived punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make 'waterproof' look like a feature of the kit; it is a raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A camera is the device a photographer uses to make pictures.

clue.text: "Mea culpa", perhaps, from a daughter with a calling

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter
a mission is a vocation or calling

explanation.surface: A daughter with a religious vocation confesses her fault.
explanation.walkthrough: Mea culpa is Latin for 'my fault', said when owning up.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying mea culpa is an example of an admission, a confession of guilt.

clue.text: Kind of tasty lemon

indicators.note: of means taken from, so the letters come out of the following words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A description of a flavourful lemon variety.
explanation.definitionFit: A style is a kind or type, as in a style of music.

clue.text: Better husbands will crack nowadays

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: AD, anno domini, marks the present era
husbands are men

explanation.surface: A claim that improved modern husbands will break down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend something is to improve it, which is to better it.

clue.text: Penelope doesn't want scribble to disappear without warning

indicators.note: not wanting something means getting rid of it, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
to pen is to write or scribble

explanation.surface: Penelope would rather her notes didn't vanish suddenly.
explanation.walkthrough: PENELOPE minus PEN leaves ELOPE.
explanation.definitionFit: To elope is to run off secretly to marry, so it is vanishing without telling anyone.

clue.text: Guard beheaded in lobby?

indicators.note: beheading cuts off the head, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: a sentry is a guard on duty

explanation.surface: A sentry decapitated in an entrance hall.
explanation.walkthrough: SENTRY loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry is an entrance hall or lobby where you first come into a building.

clue.text: Australian residents show organ as OK when damaged

indicators.note: damaged letters are knocked out of shape, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Locals in Australia report that an organ is fine after a knock.
explanation.definitionFit: Kangaroos are native Australian animals, so they are residents of that country.

clue.text: Iago was Othello's, being very old

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for an ensign or standard-bearer
second meaning: from long ago

explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Othello, Iago is called Othello's 'ancient', an archaic form of ensign.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an obsolete military rank, ensign, and also the everyday adjective for something extremely aged.

clue.text: Just depend on the setter!

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it, so the order is swapped

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as me
to depend is to rely

explanation.surface: The setter boasts that you can simply count on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depend on' looks like one phrase; split it, and 'on' places the verb after the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Merely means only or simply, as does just in 'just a moment'.
